item.title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
item.description:
Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University
During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of "Idubi" — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the "Lac de Charmes" region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area. These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than theigneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated.Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate. Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica.
Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems. As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars' hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life. Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils. Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life?
When Perseverance previously encounteredsilica-rich rocks on the inner rimof Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential. Fortunately, the rocks at "Idubi" offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway.

item.title: A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover
item.description:
This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition.
These images were taken by the Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), a camera that is also located on the end of the rover’s robotic arm. Each hole has a diameter of 0.63 inches (16 millimeters).
Curiosity was built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. JPL leads the mission on behalf of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. MAHLI was built by Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego.
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/msl-curiosity/

item.title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
item.description:
For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements.
The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position.
“Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.”
The 2026Agency Financial Reportprovides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources.
In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole.
NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time.
The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

item.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
item.description:
The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life.
Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making.
Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA.
“Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.”
His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through theArtemisprogram and ensure American leadership in space.
By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards.
As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe.
Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center.
Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis.
“My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.”
A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue.
This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him.
A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes.
“Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:How do stars form? To help answer this question,NASAused theJames Webb Space Telescopeto take thefeatured detailed imageof the star-forming regionNGC 7129ininfrared light. Star formation progresses whengravitypulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerfuljetsandwinds-- and some thenexplode. Opaquedustcan form in the coolatmospheres of starsand, when dispersed, can obstructvisible-lightimages. Many stars can be seen to be forming in thefeatured image, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right -- in the red region.Jetsandwinds likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of developmentbolsters understandingabout whatphysical processesare most important and when.Tomorrow's picture:sky duel

item.title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya
item.description:
Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.
On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers.
Positioned in the tropics beside thelargest expanse of warm ocean wateron Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “canaries in the coal mine,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants ofHumboldt Glacierin Venezuela,Quelccaya Ice Capin Peru, and theice fields of Kilimanjaroin Tanzania.
The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by theTM(Thematic Mapper) onLandsat 5(left) and in 2026 by theOLI(Operational Land Imager) onLandsat 9(right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green.
In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly2 percent of the 1988 extent. An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said.
The glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn showed a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone.
As the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each new fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice.
“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who hastracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciersin satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”
To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.
“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.
As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last.Recent satellite studiessuggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by thecurrent El Niño.
Past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the icethinned about five times faster than usual, losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from theU.S. Geological Survey.Story by Kathryn Hansen.

item.title: Outbursts from a Massive Star
item.description:
Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star located in the galaxy shown in this image released on Nov. 9, 2026.
The volatile star, known as AT 2016blu, is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, located about 30 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers estimate the mass of this star is at least 33 times that of the Sun.

item.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
item.description:
Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, onGemini XII, the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program.
In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space.
The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface.Their imageshelped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way forLandsat, was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”
For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet.
